title: Benchmarking Fraud Detectors on Private Graph Data

problem.claim: Benchmarking fraud detectors on private graph-structured data is a problem involving outsourced detector development and public communication of evaluation results.

gap.claim: Existing approaches to differentially private benchmarking do not provide utility when guaranteeing differential privacy.

contributions.claim: The paper introduces benchmarking fraud detectors on private graph-structured data as a problem.
The paper proposes a privacy attack that can de-anonymize individuals' data from evaluation results.
The paper studies two classes of differentially private benchmarking solutions and characterizes their utility trade-offs.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the benchmarking problem as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: In simulations of a privacy-sensitive NIST facial-recognition benchmark, the proposed attack achieved a True Positive Rate of 0.98 at a False Positive Rate of 0.00 for identifying whether individuals' data was present in a private dataset.
Extensive experiments found that current approaches do not provide utility when guaranteeing differential privacy.
The authors report that differential privacy error trades off between bias from distorting graph structure and variance from adding random noise.

narrative_sequence.summary: Automated fraud detection algorithms operate over graphs, and data holders may outsource detector development while evaluating submissions on private data.
Publicly communicating evaluation results creates a privacy risk because an adversary may de-anonymize individuals' data.
Simulations of a NIST facial-recognition benchmark show near-perfect reported attack accuracy, including a True Positive Rate of 0.98 at a False Positive Rate of 0.00.
The paper studies differential-privacy-based benchmarking using subsample-and-aggregate and differentially private synthetic graph data.
The reported results indicate poor utility under differential privacy and a bias-variance trade-off shaped by graph distortion, random noise, and method complexity.

source_observation.claim: Publishing evaluation results for private graph data can enable membership identification by an adversary.

interpretation.claim: Benchmark outputs should be treated as potential privacy leakage channels, not only as performance summaries.

application.claim: When designing benchmarks over sensitive graph data, evaluate whether released results support membership inference or de-anonymization.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the reported attack generalizes beyond the described simulation setting.

source_observation.claim: Differentially private benchmarking methods differ in the balance between graph-structure distortion bias and random-noise variance.

interpretation.claim: Increasing method complexity does not necessarily improve practical utility when the privacy mechanism requires high-variance noise.

application.claim: Compare privacy-preserving benchmark designs using both structural fidelity and noise-induced variability rather than privacy guarantees alone.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the formal privacy parameters, utility metrics, or conditions under which any method may remain useful.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal differential privacy parameters.
The abstract does not define the utility metrics or benchmark datasets used for the differential privacy experiments.
The abstract does not provide attack implementation details or assess generalization beyond the reported simulations.
